**The Weight of a Name**

There was a time when names carried the weight of destiny. Not the kind of destiny that fate cards whisper about—no, this was heavier. This was the kind of destiny that could make a man forget his own name.

I remember the first time I heard mine. It was in the mirror, when I was twelve, and my father had just returned from the war. He stood behind me, his breath warm against my neck, and said, *"You’re going to be a man, son. A real one."* I didn’t understand then what he meant. Now, I do.

My name was **Kaelan Veyne**. Three syllables, sharp as a blade. My father had chosen it because it sounded like a warrior’s oath. My mother had cried when she heard it, but she never said why. Maybe it was the way it rolled off the tongue like a secret. Maybe it was the way it felt like a promise.

I was good at names. I could remember them all—strangers’, teachers’, even the names of the dogs in the neighborhood. But my own? That was the one I struggled with sometimes. Not because I forgot it, but because it felt like a cage.

---

The first time I lied about my name was in the third grade.

"Who’s the new kid?" Mrs. Holloway asked, tapping her pencil against her desk.

I raised my hand. "I am," I said. "My name’s… uh… *Ethan*."

She blinked. "Ethan? That’s a nice name."

I nodded, too fast. "Yeah. It’s nice."

Ethan was safe. Ethan was ordinary. Ethan didn’t make people look at me like they were trying to guess what kind of trouble I’d get into next.

But Ethan wasn’t me.

---

By the time I was sixteen, I had at least seven names. Some were stolen—borrowed from friends who didn’t mind, or from people I’d met once and never seen again. Others I made up. **Darius**. **Rook**. **Silas**. Each one felt like a different life, a different skin.

The best one was **Veyne**.

I didn’t know where I got it. Maybe from a book. Maybe from a dream. It had a ring to it, like something out of a song. And when I used it, people listened. Not like they listened to Kaelan, who was just another kid with a mouth and a temper. Veyne made them lean in.

I used it for the first time in a bar when I was seventeen. The bouncer, a hulking man with a shaved head and a tattoo of a snake coiled around his neck, eyed me as I walked in.

"You got a name, kid?" he rumbled.

I grinned. "Veyne."

He studied me. Then, slowly, he nodded. "Yeah. You do."

And just like that, I wasn’t just another face in the crowd. I was something else.

---

But names aren’t just tools. They’re memories. They’re the voices of the people who gave them to you.

My father died when I was eighteen. He was in a car accident, drunk and reckless, just like he’d been his whole life. The police said it was an accident. My mother said it was fate.

I went to the funeral. I stood in the back, where no one would notice me. The priest spoke about redemption and grace, but all I could think about was the way my father’s hands had trembled when he tried to teach me how to hold a knife.

Afterward, my mother came up to me. She was crying, her face red and swollen. "You look just like him," she whispered.

I didn’t say anything. I didn’t know what to say.

She reached out, her fingers brushing my jaw. "Kaelan," she said, like it was a question.

I didn’t answer.

---

I spent the next five years running.

Not from the law—though I had my share of trouble. Not from the past—though I tried to forget it. But from the name itself. From the weight of it.

I changed it again and again. **Jace**. **Cade**. **Rowan**. Each one was a new start, a new chance. But none of them stuck.

Because names don’t just define you. They *are* you.

---

I found myself back in the city where I grew up one rainy Tuesday. The streets were slick, the neon signs flickering like dying stars. I was sitting on a fire escape, a cigarette between my fingers, when I heard the voice.

"Kaelan."

I didn’t turn around. I knew that voice.

"Come on, man. It’s been years."

I exhaled smoke. "Go away, Rook."

"Rook’s dead," he said. "Remember? The guy who taught you how to pick locks when you were twelve?"

I turned then. Rook was standing there, older, thinner, his once-bright eyes now dull with something I couldn’t place. "You look like hell."

I laughed. "Thanks."

He sat down beside me, close enough that I could feel the heat of him. "You ever think about why you keep changing your name?"

I didn’t answer.

"Because you’re running from something," he said. "Not from me. Not from the cops. From *him*."

I stood up. "I don’t know what you’re talking about."

Rook stood too, his hand on my shoulder. "Your father used to say the same thing. ‘Names are chains, boy. But some chains are stronger than others.’"

I pulled away. "You’re full of shit."

He shook his head. "No. I’m not. But you’re the one who’s full of fear."

---

I went home that night.

My mother was still there. She was sitting in the dark, her hands wrapped around a cup of tea. She didn’t look up when I walked in.

"Can I have some money?" I asked.

She set the cup down. "You haven’t been home in years."

"I know."

She stood up slowly. "Your father’s name was Veyne."

I froze.

She walked to the window, her back to me. "He was a good man. A bad man. But he was *his* name. And you—" She turned, her eyes wet. "You’ve been running from it."

I didn’t know what to say.

She reached into her pocket and pulled out a piece of paper. She unfolded it, revealing a single word, written in her careful handwriting:

**Veyne.**

She handed it to me.

"I don’t want it," I said.

She smiled, sad and tired. "You already do."

---

I woke up the next morning with a decision made.

I went to the police station. I told them everything. The names, the lies, the fear. They didn’t arrest me. They just listened.

Then, the detective—an old man with a face like weathered leather—leaned back in his chair. "You ever think about why you kept changing it?"

I shook my head.

He sighed. "Because you were afraid of what it meant. But names don’t define you, son. They’re just words. What you do with them—that’s what matters."

I looked down at the paper in my pocket. **Veyne.**

I folded it carefully and put it back.

---

A year later, I was standing in front of a mirror, a knife in my hand. Not to hurt anyone. To learn.

The reflection staring back at me wasn’t the boy who had run from his name. It wasn’t the man who had lied to himself for so long.

It was **Kaelan Veyne**.

And for the first time, I didn’t flinch.

---
**The End.**
